steps.name: Savra Girl
steps.text: ...You don't need to stay that far away, even if you didn't want my water.

steps.name: Savra Girl
steps.text: Did you come from the desert? Do desert folks not drink water from the forest?

steps.name: Philae
steps.text: N-No, it's not that...

steps.name: Savra Girl
steps.text: Hey, are you sure you don't need something, food and water? You look like you could collapse at any moment.

a.text: The long journey through the desert has been exhausting.
Head priest, little did I expect that I would face such trials when I decided to set out on my 'journey'.
Physical pain I could endure, but how do I answer questions like what this girl was asking me?

steps.name: Philae
steps.text: No, I'm fine... you'll get hurt.

steps.name: Savra Girl
steps.text: What?

steps.name: Philae
steps.text: (Shakes head) I hurt the things that I touch...

steps.name: Savra Girl
steps.text: Why? Are you a poison shaman?

steps.name: Philae
steps.text: No, it's not really poison... just something really troublesome...

steps.name: Savra Girl
steps.text: Figured. You look more like a priest than a poison shaman. But your horn... you're sick.

steps.name: Savra Girl
steps.text: Sick people need care.

steps.name: Philae
steps.text: Thank you... I just need some rest. I won't disturb you...

steps.name: Savra Girl
steps.text: Alright... hey, you can come back for the water later if you're thirsty! The bugs haven't gotten to the water here yet!

steps.name: Philae
steps.text: I guess this is the furthest tree from the village.

steps.name: Philae
steps.text: Let me just pop my tent down here... phew.

steps.name: Philae
steps.text: Ugh, the path's so barren. I had to make half a ration portion last for days...

steps.name: Philae
steps.text: I should get some water later. I've been in control this whole way... I wouldn't dry the well up, right?

steps.name: Philae
steps.text: I wish I was like everyone else...

steps.name: Philae
steps.text: Maybe I'd be one of those who protect the living, if I didn't know these Arts and didn't have this evil power...

steps.name: Philae
steps.text: But why did the River of Life leave me on the side of the living?

steps.name: Philae
steps.text: Ugh, there were so many things that I couldn't figure out, even when I was at the temple. There are even more of these things now that I'm out here on my own.

steps.name: Philae
steps.text: I wish I was like everyone else, so that I wouldn't have to worry about this and that... phew...

a.text: I wondered all night if I was being too sentimental.
It's not like I never thought about how people might react when I first began my journey. I didn't come out here to make friends, head priest. I came to... find answers.
But my 'journey' doesn't have a clear goal. Is that how things are supposed to go?
Perhaps it was because of thirst, or hunger. Or perhaps it was the stone tablet I was clutching that made me think of the past, of everyone.

That night, like every lonely night on the journey, I mulled over the questions that came to me repeatedly. I put my arms around myself, and gradually fell asleep to the sound of leaves rustling in the night breeze.

steps.name: Philae
steps.text: The River of Life has been generous this year, head priest. It has been a long flood season.

steps.name: Philae
steps.text: This year's harvest will be a good one.

steps.name: Philae
steps.text: Wait, why does the River of Life continue to rise when it's already so high...?

steps.name: Philae
steps.text: Head priest! Something's not right with the river...

steps.name: Philae
steps.text: Forget the ritual! Get the people out of the temple! We need to get to higher ground, go up the hills!
You're still here?

steps.name: Philae
steps.text: Huh?

steps.name: Savra Girl
steps.text: Did I wake you up? I didn't realize you were sleeping here. I thought you had left.

steps.name: Philae
steps.text: Oh, I saw you last night...

steps.name: Savra Girl
steps.text: You remember me? I'm Aisha. Are you traveling? Where are you going?

steps.name: Philae
steps.text: ...Uh, I'm Philae.

steps.name: Philae
steps.text: I... I don't actually know where I'm going.

steps.name: Aisha
steps.text: How could you not know where you're going? Anyway, I would have warned you if I knew you were gonna spend the night in the forest.

steps.name: Philae
steps.text: What?

steps.name: Aisha
steps.text: It's not safe in the forest, especially not for someone who's sick. There are locusts around.

steps.name: Philae
steps.text: Locusts?
Clack, clack.
Almost on cue, a strange sound came through the forest, rapid and fragmented.
It sounded as though something was carving wood open with sharp teeth. The sound was not particularly loud, but densely packed, like an eerie whisper that lingers in the ear.

steps.name: Aisha
steps.text: Tsk. Those damned things are at it again.

steps.name: Aisha
steps.text: Careful, they bite. Come with me to the village. Who knows when the next wave might come.

steps.name: Philae
steps.text: ...Alright, I'll come with you first.

steps.name: Philae
steps.text: That sound just now... are those Originium locusts?

a.text: I remembered that I noticed the village yesterday because it seemed glimmer in the sunlight. It looked like an oasis in the desert to my dazed eyes.
I looked past Aisha's shoulder at the strange gleam that appeared in the forest.
Grey-white crystals began creeping up the branches, covering up the once-lush leaves. Bulging veins underneath the bark gradually grew, like some kind of lesion.
Several dead Originium locusts lay on the ground, covered in a thin layer of crystalline dust. They struck fear into my heart even without any sign of movement.

steps.name: Aisha
steps.text: You ever seen it before? These bugs have been plaguing the ancestral forest for years.

steps.name: Aisha
steps.text: They're no ordinary locusts. These evil things chew through steel, water sources, and the hearts of trees!

steps.name: Philae
steps.text: The locusts have been around for a while? Is there a way to drive them out?

steps.name: Aisha
steps.text: We make pesticides in the village. I was spreading them in the forests just now.

steps.name: Aisha
steps.text: We used to be able to kill plenty of bugs with it, but it doesn't work so well now...

steps.name: Aisha
steps.text: Those things aren't afraid of fire. You can't chase them away, and they don't care if you're crying or praying.

steps.name: Aisha
steps.text: Besides, we can't use fire in the ancestral forest... these trees are holy to our village, and we can't afford to accidentally burn them.

steps.name: Aisha
steps.text: Ah, looks like the sunlight's getting brighter. I forgot to tell you last night, but it's not safe in the forest during the day. The village's this way. Keep up with me.

steps.name: Aisha
steps.text: ...The caravans all say that the ancestral forest looks like an emerald from a distance!

steps.name: Aisha
steps.text: Besides, the ancestral forest used to be MUCH bigger than it is now! People wouldn't let their kids go into the forest on their own, because it's really easy to get lost.

steps.name: Aisha
steps.text: Hehe, I was always a careless kid. The adults wouldn't let me out of their sight when I went into the forest with them, lest I do something to offend the ancestors and gods.

steps.name: Aisha
steps.text: The ancestral forest watches over us, granting us food and water. We would not survive without its blessing...

steps.name: Aisha
steps.text: But we hardly go into the forest anymore. There are Originium locusts about during the day, so we only go out at night.

steps.name: Aisha
steps.text: Oh, but this path's safe, don't worry! I've walked it many times, and never encountered Originium locusts during the day.

steps.name: Philae
steps.text: (Whisper) Almost all the trees along the path are crystallized. The locusts got them... even the grass has wilted.

steps.name: Aisha
steps.text: This area has been abandoned for a long time. It used to be stockbeast pastures, but the rocks that appeared out of the ground make it impossible for grass to grow.

steps.name: Aisha
steps.text: People were forced to sell or kill their stockbeasts. I remember how the children cried for days...

steps.name: Philae
steps.text: How could this be... this place has been affected by Originium for so long...?

a.text: I looked down sadly at the lifeless twigs on the ground.

steps.name: Philae
steps.text: Poor things... they were choked to death by Originium crystals.

steps.name: Philae
steps.text: (Whisper) All things living should be allowed to live quietly under the sun, like how flowers bloom, how fruits become ripe, and how animals grow big... the Originium consumes it all.

steps.name: Philae
steps.text: They didn't even have the chance to refuse.

steps.name: Aisha
steps.text: You're more sentimental than I thought. Are all priests like that?

steps.name: Aisha
steps.text: I can see where you're coming from, though. It's the same for people in the village. It's not food that we're most worried about.

steps.name: Aisha
steps.text: It's how the poor forest is being destroyed, and the living things that had been with us for so long are taken away, without even a chance to protect themselves.

steps.name: Philae
steps.text: (...If it was the power of healing that I had... could I restore the crystallized parts?)

steps.name: Philae
steps.text: (Or at least, alleviate the trees' pain.)

steps.name: Aisha
steps.text: Why are you so far behind me? Keep up, we're almost there.

steps.name: Philae
steps.text: The crystallized trees... I'm not familiar with Originium locusts, but I've seen those crystals a lot.

steps.name: Philae
steps.text: The trees that we passed are dangerous. If you continue to live in this environment...

steps.name: Aisha
steps.text: Hey, what's going on? Why is everyone outside?

steps.name: Worried Villager
steps.text: The damage to the forest just keeps getting worse. We may not have enough food to last the year.

steps.name: Worried Villager
steps.text: And we're running out of things to trade with the caravans...

steps.name: Impatient Villager
steps.text: I told you we should have increased the dosage of the pesticide! The amount we're using doesn't do anything!

steps.name: Worried Villager
steps.text: It's a poison. Too much of it could harm the trees. The trees at the grove that I used to pick berries from have all died.

steps.name: Impatient Villager
steps.text: It was the locusts that did it, not the pesticide!

steps.name: Impatient Villager
steps.text: I don't even dare go near the berry trees these days. A couple of days ago I saw a nest of beastlings lying there. They weren't moving... my kid used to draw their pictures...

steps.name: Mayor
steps.text: Friends... perhaps it's really time for us to leave.

steps.name: Mayor
steps.text: The locusts have been getting worse each year. They'll devour the whole ancestral forest at this rate.

steps.name: Mayor
steps.text: We tried asking nearby villages for help, but the locusts are so many and so fierce, attacking the people who came to help... no one wants to come anymore.

steps.name: Aisha
steps.text: Wait, why are we talking about moving away?

steps.name: Philae
steps.text: Aisha! Wait—

steps.name: Aisha
steps.text: And just abandon the ancestral forest? I'm not leaving. You want to leave, you can do it on your own.

steps.name: Aisha
steps.text: I'll look for casters from other villages, other towns. There must be a way to kill those bugs and heal the sick trees!

steps.name: Mayor
steps.text: Aisha? No... it's not so simple...

steps.name: Aisha
steps.text: I've been out spreading pesticide since morning, going through the whole forest... there are still many healthy trees left!

steps.name: Mayor
steps.text: I don't want our traditions to end with me either... but we need to find a way to survive.

steps.name: Impatient Villager
steps.text: Do you know how far the nearest water source is? Maybe we could survive the journey, but the children won't.

steps.name: Worried Villager
steps.text: We stayed here because the ancestral forest is here, because our water source is here. How do we survive if we leave? Our lives depend on the forest.

steps.name: Mayor
steps.text: If only there was another way...

a.text: —I was suddenly reminded of the River of Life.
I could see it even without closing my eyes.
As the villagers argued, the forest and the village became the temple, the river banks, the farmland, the source of life that I defended and revered.
We stood on top of the hill, gazing down at the wall of murky water surging through. It made the temple seem so small, so fragile.
I thought the wind-worn stones would survive the century under the scorching sun.
I never thought the flood would take them so easily, like cube sugars melting in coffee.
Now I stand before another village about to be swallowed by fate, listening to arguments so familiar they might as well have been from another dream.
I told myself to stay still. Don't interfere. There was nothing I could do to heal their ills.
But––

steps.name: Philae
steps.text: Traditions don't mean anything if there's nobody left to protect them.

steps.name: Philae
steps.text: I know a passing traveler like me shouldn't interfere with your village's matters.

steps.name: Philae
steps.text: But those crystals are very dangerous... they're going to spread, and it'll be too late by the time they start appearing near the houses!
Clack, clack.

steps.name: Philae
steps.text: I know you don't want to abandon your faith. But the forest bestowed its blessings so that you could live.

steps.name: Philae
steps.text: If you want... I could protect you on your way to finding another water source—

steps.name: Aisha
steps.text: What are you saying, Philae? Why are you on the mayor's side?

steps.name: Aisha
steps.text: This forest was an oasis that the gods promised us. Abandoning it means going back on our oath... that's what truly brings disaster!
Clack, clack.

steps.name: Mayor
steps.text: No need to be hasty, Aisha. We're still discussing this.

steps.name: Aisha
steps.text: You guys kept telling me to remember the legends of the forest and its blessings. It's you who's forgotten them, isn't it?

steps.name: Mayor
steps.text: Wait, that's...!
Clack, clack.

a.text: Perhaps I had let my awareness as a guardian slip, and allowed myself to wallow in sentimentality and hesitation.
That was why I failed to notice that sound, coming in every direction, almost like the echoes of leaves rustling in the wind.
It was an adult locust. Its abdomen was grey-white in color, and its wings were filled with cracks. It flew screeching into the village, like the dagger of the god of death.
It was only inches away from Aisha by the time I heard the hungry buzzing of its wings—

steps.name: Aisha
steps.text: What the...?

steps.name: Philae
steps.text: Ugh!

steps.name: Philae
steps.text: Got there in time... are you alright, Aisha? Looks like a small scratch. I have some herbs here...

steps.name: Aisha
steps.text: Huh...?

steps.name: Impatient Villager
steps.text: Look! That locust on the ground...

steps.name: Impatient Villager
steps.text: Did it... shrivel up?

steps.name: Worried Villager
steps.text: I saw patterns appear on the ground when it hit the traveler's stone tablet... is that Arts?

steps.name: Worried Villager
steps.text: Is this the caster you found, Aisha? Are we saved?

steps.name: Philae
steps.text: I-I'm sorry, I lost control for an instant... I'm sorry...

steps.name: Philae
steps.text: I didn't mean to...

steps.name: Aisha
steps.text: What are you apologizing for? You knew a way to destroy Originium locusts? Why didn't you tell us?

a.text: My mouth was open but I didn't know what to say, so all I could do was stare at Aisha, who was staring at the dead Originium locust on the ground, her eyes filled with surprise and joy.

steps.name: Aisha
steps.text: Wow... you shriveled up a huge bug like that with one hit! That was amazing, Philae!

steps.name: Philae
steps.text: It's not like that...

steps.name: Mayor
steps.text: Everybody okay?! Get inside! The locusts are on the move!

steps.name: Mayor
steps.text: You come too, traveler.

steps.name: Philae
steps.text: ...So you see, it's not a good power.

steps.name: Aisha
steps.text: But you saved me and took out that locust!

steps.name: Philae
steps.text: It's the power of death and destruction! It can't heal the village!

steps.name: Aisha
steps.text: Isn't killing the locusts just like healing the forest?

steps.name: Philae
steps.text: ...If I missed by just a little bit, it might have been you who withered, instead of the locust.

steps.name: Aisha
steps.text: But you managed to control it, didn't you?

steps.name: Mayor
steps.text: ...Traveler, you're the only sign of hope that we've seen in the last few years.

steps.name: Mayor
steps.text: Your Arts just saved someone. We saw it with our own eyes.

steps.name: Mayor
steps.text: I know it's a lot to ask, but we're desperate for any solution. If you could just try... maybe it'll change something...

steps.name: Philae
steps.text: I don't know... please, give me some time to think.

steps.name: Philae
steps.text: *pant* *pant*... no one saw me sneak out, right?

steps.name: Philae
steps.text: This is... the tree where I took shelter last night. Still no crystals... looks like you survived the Originium locusts for another day.

steps.name: Philae
steps.text: *sigh* I just don't know what to think... ended up sneaking out when the others split up to find food.

steps.name: Philae
steps.text: How could I possibly say yes? They'll be even sadder if something happens to the forest, especially Aisha who loves it so much.

steps.name: Philae
steps.text: I've never used Arts on such a scale, not to mention that I have to be precise and not harm any other living things... ahh, even the thought makes it nervous! I can't do it!

steps.name: Philae
steps.text: No, I can't just run away quietly. I have to go back and explain to the others that... I just can't do it...

steps.name: Philae
steps.text: But... what would happen to the village if I left without helping them? Today it was a few locusts. What happens tomorrow?

steps.name: Philae
steps.text: What do I do, head priest...
Over here! I found her!

steps.name: Philae
steps.text: What...?

steps.name: Impatient Villager
steps.text: She's here! I think she's trying to run away!

steps.name: Philae
steps.text: Run away? No, I...

steps.name: Impatient Villager
steps.text: You can't go! If you leave now, my child... you can destroy those locusts! You've already done it once!

steps.name: Worried Villager
steps.text: Why do you give us hope, if you're not here to help us?

steps.name: Impatient Villager
steps.text: If you really make everything you touch 'wither', why was Aisha unharmed when you picked her up after she fell? I saw it with my own eyes!

steps.name: Philae
steps.text: I didn't! I can't...

steps.name: Philae
steps.text: I already explained it...

steps.name: Worried Villager
steps.text: Uh, why do you keep talking like your ability is some kind of curse? Maybe I should put it another way... can you make that grass wither?

steps.name: Philae
steps.text: I can't do this to an innocent living thing just to prove something!

steps.name: Worried Villager
steps.text: If you left now, how would you be different from the other casters who just abandoned us without even trying? Please, don't go...

steps.name: Philae
steps.text: No! D-Don't touch me!

steps.name: Impatient Villager
steps.text: Is helping us really so hard? We can talk about payment if that's the issue!

steps.name: Philae
steps.text: No...

steps.name: Aisha
steps.text: Hey! What are you guys doing? Don't press her like this!

steps.name: Philae
steps.text: I'm sorry, Aisha, but I can't try it on your ancestral forest... I'm scared that it would make things worse for the village...

steps.name: Aisha
steps.text: I don't understand, Philae... Why do you always take a step back?

steps.name: Philae
steps.text: Huh...?

steps.name: Aisha
steps.text: You wouldn't take my water and kept your distance from me when walking. You said you weren't a poison shaman and said you bring destruction.

steps.name: Aisha
steps.text: Life is not as fragile as you think it is, Philae.

steps.name: Philae
steps.text: Did I... disappoint everyone again?

steps.name: Philae
steps.text: Is there a meaning for everyone's existence, head priest? What's the meaning of mine, then?

steps.name: Philae
steps.text: You said I would find my path. But at the end of the day, my powers can only be used to 'take away life', not 'give it'.

steps.name: Philae
steps.text: The nature of my powers cannot be changed, no matter how much I try to control myself and my Arts.

steps.name: Philae
steps.text: The trials that you gave me always led to death... so I learned to control, suppress, stay away.

steps.name: Philae
steps.text: But what then?

steps.name: Philae
steps.text: I couldn't let it go, but what could I do...

steps.name: Philae
steps.text: Poor trees. It must hurt to have crystals growing all over you.

steps.name: Philae
steps.text: Everyone's heart must have hurt when Aisha stopped the mayor, when the villagers struggled, and when the mayor talked about moving away.

steps.name: Philae
steps.text: What were you thinking when we looked down at the River of Life, head priest?

steps.name: Philae
steps.text: I don't want my Arts to take any life... it's the power of destruction, and that which is born in nature should not be ended by this human force...

steps.name: Philae
steps.text: Head priest, I've never thought of any creature as being inherently evil. Even these locusts might have been innocent victims of the influence of Originium.

steps.name: Philae
steps.text: But I see and feel even greater pain, and endless destruction.

steps.name: Philae
steps.text: This land and this forest deserve to live their lives and futures to the fullest.

steps.name: Philae
steps.text: But the locusts are like a plague, spreading uncontrollably. The pain they brought far exceeds the need for their own survival. Is destruction the sole reason for their existence?

steps.name: Philae
steps.text: And what about me, head priest? For what purpose do my past, present and future exist?

steps.name: Philae
steps.text: ...No, I must not cry.

steps.name: Philae
steps.text: The locusts are spreading too fast. If I hesitate any longer, the village, the forest, everything here... these innocent lives have already suffered too much.

steps.name: Philae
steps.text: The mayor was right. They won't need to live in fear anymore if they move away. There'll be a way, as long as life goes on. There will be new hope in their new home.

steps.name: Philae
steps.text: Besides... it wouldn't be the mayor's fault that the village's tradition ended, if I was the one who did it.

steps.name: Philae
steps.text: I can't allow the crystals to continue spreading. I'll take responsibility and help them find a new water source...

steps.name: Philae
steps.text: Is this the meaning of my existence, head priest?

steps.name: Philae
steps.text: No time to think. The sun's about to rise.

a.text: So I put my hands on the ground and breathed out.
It was quiet all around, but I could feel something gathering in the forest, something struggling violently deep below the surface.
A thin mist began to rise from the ground. It was not cold air, but a curious silence, as time seemed to be suppressed on an invisible waterline by my will.
The crystals began to shatter.

Cracks began to appear on the trees on the outside, spreading from the trunks to the branches. As the last bit of lifeforce was wiped away, the Originium crystals lost their support and fell to the ground.
I heard more sounds of shattering coming from the distance. Head priest, this time I didn't close my eyes, like I did in the previous trials.
I watched as the crystallized trees began to wilt, no longer forced to keep themselves upright; I watched locusts fly out and wither in mid-air, dropping to the ground like falling snow.
Tears streamed from my eyes, rolling silently down towards the ground shaking beneath my hands, into this funeral of my making with no other witness.
Only when there was no other sound in the forest did I pull my hands back. The marks of casting were still there upon them.
Do you know, head priest? I saw them clearly for the first time.

steps.name: Philae
steps.text: The forest is quiet... no sound of wings buzzing, or Originium crystals growing.

steps.name: Philae
steps.text: It's over.

steps.name: Philae
steps.text: May you rest in peace, free from the control of Originium, never again to become an instrument of destruction. May you be free.

steps.name: Philae
steps.text: I'm sorry, blessed trees. All I can do is lay my hand on you... you're free now, never again to feel pain.

steps.name: Philae
steps.text: Phew... I'll wait a little longer, then go back to the village and admit what I did...

steps.name: Philae
steps.text: Huh?
Rustle, rustle.

steps.name: Philae
steps.text: ...The sound of leaves rustling in the wind?

steps.name: Philae
steps.text: What's going on... some trees are still alive here... and over there...

steps.name: Philae
steps.text: Don't my Arts cause everything to wither?

steps.name: Philae
steps.text: How could this be... the destruction that I brought didn't touch every living thing?

steps.name: Philae
steps.text: How could this be... are you real?

steps.name: Aisha
steps.text: Life is not as fragile as you think it is, Philae.

steps.name: Philae
steps.text: Shouldn't I help with the rebuilding of the temple?

steps.name: Head Priest
steps.text: Hah, worried that we wouldn't do a good job?

steps.name: Philae
steps.text: N-No, that's not what I mean...

steps.name: Head Priest
steps.text: Life is not as fragile as you think it is, Philae.

steps.name: Head Priest
steps.text: The River of Life may have inundated the farms on the banks. But the flood will pass, and the sediment it leaves behind will become fertile soil and nurture new life.

steps.name: Head Priest
steps.text: The cycle of life goes on.

steps.name: Philae
steps.text: But that's because it's the River of Life. It always brings new life.

steps.name: Head Priest
steps.text: So can you, Philae. You can bring life too. Otherwise, why are we standing here, alive and breathing?

steps.name: Head Priest
steps.text: Trust yourself, and trust life. It's not as fragile as you think it is.

a.text: Only then did I remember what you said to me before I left, head priest.
I couldn't help but reach out to the trees that still lived. I tried to pull my hand back as I realized what I was doing, when a butterfly landed on my fingertip.
The sun began to rise, casting its light upon the forest, and it was exactly as Aisha said it was.
The butterfly glowed blue like a jewel. It shook its feelers a couple of times, then flew away without withering.
Do you know, head priest? My fingertip... itched a little. I discovered that the feeling of being near a living thing was itchy.

steps.name: Philae
steps.text: Well, it's time to leave. The weather is good. That's a good start.

steps.name: Philae
steps.text: This will be far enough, Aisha.

steps.name: Aisha
steps.text: Are you sure you just want some writing tools and paper? I made these rations. Take it with you.

steps.name: Philae
steps.text: I'll be fine, I have enough on me.

steps.name: Philae
steps.text: Besides, I never cleared up the misunderstanding with the other villagers... I never did any 'cleansing'. I can't accept gifts that I don't deserve.

steps.name: Aisha
steps.text: You priests are so humble... don't forget to write to me, then! And tell me when you figure out where you're going.

steps.name: Philae
steps.text: Yes, I will. Before that, though, I need to write home. Thanks to you guys, I've made discoveries that I can't wait to share—

a.text: I apologize, head priest, but I need to say this again—I'm going on a journey again. Farewell.

There are still a lot of things that I don't understand, but I think I've figured out why I'm setting out on this journey, what I'm looking for, and what I can do, not just for the answer, but also to come to terms with myself.
I locked my own possibilities away in a little box. I was afraid to touch it, and afraid that it would touch others. That's why I was confused and hesitant.
But the events of the past several days made me realize that it's okay to touch...
